title: A court of poets at Anandpur
hookLine: the young Guru gathers poets and scholars, writes himself, and fights at Bhangani in 1688

lines: AND A COURT FULL OF POETS.
cards: Nine years old, a father executed in Delhi, and a whole community now looking to you. A child like that could grow up hard, angry, all armor. The young Guru Gobind Rai did grow up strong.
He trained in riding, archery and the sword, and the hill rajas around Anandpur watched him with suspicion. But he also did something unexpected.
He filled his court with poets: musicians, scholars, translators, writers of every background, and he wrote alongside them.

teach.b: Tradition says the Guru kept fifty-two poets at his court.
They translated old stories and epics into the language people spoke, wrote verse about heroes and about God, and made Anandpur, a small hill town, a center of learning.

teach.h: THE GURU WRITES IN THREE LANGUAGES.
teach.b: The Guru himself wrote in several languages: Braj, a literary Hindi of the time, Persian, and Punjabi.

For some years he lived at Paonta, a quiet spot on the Yamuna river, where tradition says much of his early poetry was written. Many of his writings were later gathered into the Dasam Granth, the book of the tenth.
Many Sikhs recite some of its hymns daily, like the Jaap Sahib. Scholars and Sikhs discuss how much of the whole collection comes from the Guru's own pen, and that conversation continues.
Then, in 1688, the sword. A hill raja, Fateh Shah, with allied rajas, marched against the Guru, and they met at Bhangani, near Paonta. The Guru's force was small, and here Sikhs keep a detail.

teach.h: PIR BUDHU SHAH FIGHTS BESIDE HIM.
teach.b: A Muslim Sufi saint, Pir Budhu Shah, came to fight on the Guru's side, with his sons and hundreds of his followers. Tradition says two of his sons were killed in the battle.
The Guru won, and tradition says he thanked the Pir with his own comb, strands of his hair still in it, and a turban.
The young Guru held both, the pen and the sword, and neither canceled the other. The poet fought. The fighter wrote about God.

how: Many Sikhs recite the Jaap Sahib, attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, in their daily morning prayers, and Paonta Sahib on the Yamuna is visited as the place where he wrote much of his poetry.

games.q: you're Pir Budhu Shah, a Sufi saint. the young Guru is outnumbered by the hill rajas. what do you do?
o: stay out of it: it isn't your fight.
bring your sons and followers to fight beside him.
send a letter asking for peace.

practice: Take one line of poetry: a hymn, a song you love, even a line you half remember. Say it slowly, then again slower, letting each word land. Then close your eyes and let it echo while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Dasam Granth. The book of the tenth, gathering much of Guru Gobind Singh's own writing, from the years his court at Anandpur was full of poets.
